title: The ascetics I have seen
hookLine: the poet has seen hosts of monks, siddhas and yogis, yet without love for the Lord it is all worth nothing (Savaiye 1)

lines: A TRAVELER WHO HAS SEEN THEM ALL.
cards: A traveler has made it his business to see every holy person in the land. He's sat outside the huts of ascetics who've given up everything. He's watched yogis hold impossible postures for hours.
He's met celibates, wonder-workers, wandering monks, holy men of every order. Some could do things you and I can't.
At the end of all that traveling, he sits down to write what he's learned, and it comes out in one breath.

teach.h: HE HAS SEEN EVERY KIND OF HOLY ONE.
teach.b: That traveler is the voice of the first savaiya. In paraphrase: I have wandered and seen hosts of pure ascetics, siddhas, the dwellings of yogis and celibates.
I have seen heroes and gods and sages, the holy men of sect after sect, the religious ways of every country.
Then the last line turns: without the love and grace of the Lord, all of this isn't worth one ratti. A ratti is a tiny red seed, used as a small weight for gold.
So the verse puts the whole parade of holiness on a jeweler's scale, and without love the pan doesn't tip. This is easy to hear wrong.
It isn't sneering at discipline; the poet went out to see these people. Sikh teaching favors the householder's life over the cave, but this verse doesn't sneer at those who chose the cave.

Its point is narrower and harder. A person can sit for years, give up food, give up sleep, and if love isn't at the center, the verse says it's weightless. And it isn't only about other people's practices.

Sikhs often hear it as a mirror: early rising, long recitations, a person's own discipline can go on the same scale. Said in the morning, before the day's practice begins, the verse asks what's at the center.

how: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya each morning as the first of the ten Tav Prasad Savaiye, and it is often explained in the gurdwara as a warning against outward religion without love.

o: strict discipline kept for many years
a vow to give up home and family

games.q: the first savaiya — tap the pairs.
p: has seen every kind of holy one
when many Sikhs say this verse

s: the first savaiya mocks people who practice discipline
it respects them enough to travel to see them. its point is that without love, even great discipline weighs nothing.
a ratti is a tiny seed once used as a jeweler's weight
the verse weighs all that holiness against the smallest weight there was.
Sikhs hear the verse only as being about other people's practices
it is often heard as a mirror: a person's own discipline goes on the same scale.

games.q: you're the traveler. you have seen ascetics, yogis, monks and holy men of every order. you sit down to write what it all adds up to. what do you write?
o: without love, none of it is worth a single ratti.
games.why: the savaiya weighs the whole parade of holiness and finds it weighs nothing without the love and grace of the Lord. it doesn't call anyone a fraud.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you'll do today that could be done either way: making someone's coffee, answering a hard message, helping at home.

Picture it done for show, wanting it noticed, keeping a little count; then picture it done for the person, with nothing in it for you, and feel how different the two are. If you pray, let Waheguru rest on your breath.

wordCard.voice: Prem, love. In the first savaiya, a traveler sees every kind of holy discipline, and without love weighs it all at less than one ratti, a jeweler's tiny seed.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: prem, love. what this verse finds missing from the parade.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing without love. Love is what tips the scale. Day three hundred sixty-three.
